title: 05. Retrieval, Hybrid & Reranking: Why Reranking Is Needed
summary: ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) retrieval with bi-encoder embeddings is fast and scalable, but imprecise: the top-K results are approximately sorted by semantic similarity, and rank 1 is not always truly the most relevant document.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body: ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) retrieval with bi-encoder embeddings is fast and scalable, but imprecise: the top-K results are approximately sorted by semantic similarity, and rank 1 is not always truly the most relevant document. This imprecision has two sources: (1) ANN search itself may skip the exact nearest neighbor in exchange for speed; (2) bi-encoder embeddings represent query and document independently, without joint reasoning about the relevance of a specific document to a specific query. Reranking is the step that follows initial retrieval — it takes the top-50 to top-100 roughly relevant candidates from the bi-encoder retrieval and applies a more expensive, more precise relevance scorer to reorder them. The top-K of the reranked results (typically K=3-10) are then sent to the LLM.

diagrams.title: Two-stage retrieval: recall first, precision second
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[("1M chunks")] --> S1["Stage 1: fast retriever — top 50, ~20 ms"]
  S1 --> S2["Stage 2: cross-encoder reranker — scores 50 pairs, ~150 ms"]
  S2 --> K["keep top 4–5"] --> LLM["LLM"]
diagrams.explain: The first stage is tuned for **recall** (do not miss the right chunk); the reranker is tuned for **precision** (put it first). Rerankers are too slow for a million documents but perfect for 50 — and passing fewer, better chunks makes the answer cheaper and more accurate.

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
TWO-STAGE RETRIEVAL + RERANKING PIPELINE
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STAGE 1: BI-ENCODER RETRIEVAL (fast, approximate)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Query: "What items are excluded from the warranty?"

Pre-computed doc embeddings in vector DB:
  D1: [warranty coverage defects]  → score 0.91
  D2: [warranty terms conditions]  → score 0.89
  D3: [warranty exclusions list]   → score 0.88 ← MOST RELEVANT (rank 3!)
  D4: [product replacement policy] → score 0.84
  D5: [customer service contact]   → score 0.72

Bi-encoder returns D1, D2, D3, D4, D5 (sorted by approximate score)
D3 is rank 3 even though it's most relevant → bi-encoder imprecision!

STAGE 2: CROSS-ENCODER RERANKING (slow, precise)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Cross-encoder processes (query, document) pairs with full attention:

query="What items are excluded from warranty?"

[QUERY] [SEP] [D1: "Warranty covers manufacturing defects for 2 years"]
  → Cross-attention: "excluded" ↔ "covers" (opposite meaning!)
  → Score: 3.2 (low relevance — talks about what IS covered, not excluded)

[QUERY] [SEP] [D3: "Warranty exclusions: physical damage, water damage, normal wear"]
  → Cross-attention: "excluded" ↔ "exclusions" (strong match!)
  → Score: 9.1 (HIGH relevance — directly lists exclusions!)

POST-RERANKING ORDER:
  Rank 1: D3 (exclusions list)  — score 9.1  ← CORRECTLY PROMOTED ✓
  Rank 2: D2 (terms conditions) — score 7.4
  Rank 3: D1 (coverage defects) — score 3.2
  Rank 4: D4 (replacement)      — score 2.8
  Rank 5: D5 (contact)          — score 1.1

RERANKER MODEL COMPARISON (2026):
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Model                      Latency   Quality   Cost      Tokens
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cross-encoder MiniLM-L-6   50ms      Good      Free      512
cross-encoder MiniLM-L-12  100ms     Better    Free      512
BGE Reranker v2-m3         150ms     Excellent Free      512
Cohere Rerank v3           200ms     Best      $$$       4096
GPT-4o (listwise)          2000ms    Best      $$$$      128K
Jina Reranker v2           120ms     Excellent Free      8192

RRF vs SCORE FUSION:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
System 1 scores (dense):  [0.91, 0.85, 0.72, 0.68, 0.61]
System 2 scores (sparse): [18.2, 12.1, 5.4, 4.1, 2.8]

Score fusion: normalize both → weighted average
  Problem: outlier in sparse scores dominates!

RRF (rank-based): 1/(60+rank)
  System 1 ranks: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  System 2 ranks: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  (different score scales become irrelevant — only rank matters)
  → Robust to outlier scores ✓
  → No normalization needed ✓
```

Cross-encoder: fast (100-500ms for 100 docs), cheap, good accuracy.
Cross-encoders require joint encoding of the query+document pair in a single forward pass — they cannot pre-compute document representations.
quiz.explanation: Cross-encoders require joint encoding of the query+document pair in a single forward pass — they cannot pre-compute document representations. For a corpus of 1M documents, a cross-encoder would need 1M forward passes per query, each taking ~50ms → 50,000 seconds per query.

quiz.question: What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion and how does it differ from score-based reranking?
options: Pairwise: compare pairs of documents, determine which is more relevant (RankNet, RankSVM).
Passage-level: rerank individual chunks (default in RAG — each chunk is a passage).
The "candidate pool" for reranking should be 10x-20x the final desired K.
RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) is a rank-based fusion method that doesn't use raw scores at all — it only uses the position (rank) of each result in each retrieval list.
quiz.explanation: RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) is a rank-based fusion method that doesn't use raw scores at all — it only uses the position (rank) of each result in each retrieval list. RRF_score(d) = Σ 1/(k + rank_i(d)) for each retrieval method i. Benefits: (1) no score normalization needed across heterogeneous systems; (2) robust to outlier scores; (3) empirically excellent despite simplicity.

NDCG@K (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain), MRR@K (Mean Reciprocal Rank), and Precision@K.

quiz.explanation: Cross-encoder: fast (100-500ms for 100 docs), cheap, good accuracy. LLM-based: slow (1-5s), expensive ($0.10-0.50 per query), best accuracy. Use cross-encoder for real-time applications; LLM-based for offline batch processing, document review systems, or very high-stakes retrieval where accuracy is paramount.

quiz.explanation: The "candidate pool" for reranking should be 10x-20x the final desired K. If you want K=5 final results, pass 50-100 candidates to the reranker. Too few: reranker has nothing better to promote.
